target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers and let more Americans vote
objection: Federal holidays do not require private employers to give paid time off, and many low-income workers in retail and service jobs would still be scheduled to work, so the holiday would not reliably remove the practical voting barrier for them.

target: AG1’s implication that making Election Day a holiday would help low-income workers rather than harm them
objection: If low-income workers still have to work on Election Day, they may lose wages or have to absorb unpaid time off, so the policy could disadvantage them instead of helping them.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would meaningfully increase turnout on its own
objection: Research suggests that an election-day holiday by itself is not an especially effective way to raise turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1’s argument that Election Day should be a holiday because it is a workable policy and could be paired with other reforms
objection: More reliable solutions exist, especially state-level employer voting-leave rules and automatic voter registration, so a holiday is not the best primary reform.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not reliably help low-income workers because they might still have to work
objection: On federal holidays many schools close and many workplaces reduce hours or close, so a holiday would make Election Day a less typical school/work day for many people, including many low-income workers.

target: AG2’s assumption that the main barrier is still lost wages or unpaid leave even if the day is a holiday
objection: For many voters, the key barrier is simply being required to be at school or work during voting hours; if Election Day is a non-working or reduced-work day, people can vote without requesting extra time off or missing work as much.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would still disadvantage low-income workers
objection: Because the holiday reduces whether voters must miss work or class, it would lessen the specific scheduling constraint that blocks low-income voters from participating rather than clearly disadvantaging them.

target: AG2’s argument that automatic voter registration or other reforms are preferable and that a holiday is not enough
objection: Other reforms can be pursued alongside a holiday, so the fact that a holiday alone is not sufficient does not mean Election Day should not also be made a holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not meaningfully improve access because some workers still would not get paid time off
objection: Even if paid time off is not guaranteed everywhere, a holiday can still reduce the need to be at school or work and therefore improve access to voting for many people.

target: AG2’s suggestion that the holiday is ineffective because it does not fix pre-Election Day registration problems
objection: The holiday is aimed at day-of scheduling barriers, while early voting and absentee voting can be used for those who plan ahead, so the holiday still addresses a major access problem even if it does not solve every registration issue.

target: AG2’s assumption that weekend/holiday election timing is not workable just because paid time off is not guaranteed
objection: Many other OECD democracies hold elections on weekends or holidays, which indicates that this timing is administratively workable and commonly used.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday timing does not really improve access
objection: The comparison with other OECD countries supports the inference that weekend or holiday election timing does reduce real voting-access barriers, not merely create the appearance of access.

target: AG2’s claim that the chief issue is pre-Election Day administrative hurdles rather than day-of availability
objection: For many voters, the main problem is being unable to vote during the Election Day window because school or work overlaps with polling hours, so changing the day itself still matters.

target: AG2’s claim that early voting and absentee voting make a holiday unnecessary
objection: A national holiday can increase attention to the election and encourage more people to plan around voting, including using advance voting options, so it can complement rather than be replaced by early or absentee voting.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income voters are mainly affected by wages rather than schedule timing
objection: Low-income voters are also affected by school and caregiving schedules during the day, so the barrier is broader than just lost wages.

target: AG2’s assumption that a holiday would not help caregivers or parents
objection: If schools are likely to close or operate differently on a national holiday, caregivers and parents would face fewer daytime school, daycare, and caregiving conflicts when trying to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday makes voting a celebration and thereby increases participation
objection: There is no direct reason to think changing Election Day into a holiday would itself make people more likely to participate; the main effect could still be symbolic rather than practical.

target: AG1’s claim that broad public support makes the policy reasonable
objection: Popular support alone does not show that the policy is the best or most effective way to improve turnout.

target: AG1’s comparison to other OECD countries as evidence that the policy is workable
objection: The fact that other countries use weekend or holiday elections does not prove that the same approach would solve U.S. turnout or access problems in practice.
